title: ‘CM Vijay’ WhatsApp call promises Rs 11 lakh aid, Bengaluru man loses Rs 1 lakh

reading.body:
This is an impersonation fraud carried out with a synthetic video call. The face and voice on the call were generated to resemble a public figure, and the entire scheme depended on the target believing he was speaking to that person. The deepfake was not the payload of the attack, it was the door: it established enough trust for the caller to hand the victim off to supposed intermediaries who then extracted money in stages.

The failure sits at the point of contact between a real-time communication channel and a user with no way to verify who is on the other end. WhatsApp video calls carry no authentication of identity, and a convincing synthetic likeness defeats the ordinary cues a person uses to judge whether a caller is genuine. Catching this would have required either a verification step outside the call, such as confirming the offer through an official channel, or platform-level signals that the video stream was synthetic. Neither was present.

What is not established is who produced the deepfake, how it was made, or whether the people who demanded the payments were connected to whoever generated the video. The police registered a case under the Information Technology Act, and a case is not a finding of guilt.

reports.title: ‘CM Vijay’ WhatsApp call promises Rs 11 lakh aid, Bengaluru man loses Rs 1 lakh

summary:
A 29-year-old security guard in Bengaluru named Ratikanta Giri received a WhatsApp video call on September 9 from someone using a deepfake video to pose as Tamil Nadu Chief Minister Vijay. The caller offered him Rs 11 lakh in financial aid and said a manager would arrange the transfer. The manager then demanded fees, including Rs 5,000 as exchange charges and Rs 18,000 to unlock a PIN. Another person claiming to be a CBI officer demanded over Rs 50,000 as a fine. Giri paid over Rs 1.04 lakh through a digital payment app before refusing a further Rs 50,000 demand and realizing he had been cheated.

Giri contacted the cybercrime helpline 1930 and then approached Byappanahalli police, who registered a case under the Information Technology Act. This is the first such deepfake case reported in the city. A senior officer urged people not to believe such calls or make payments based on similar claims.
